Mechanistic insights from mouse models: Inosine directly inhibits the ubiquitin-activating enzyme UBA6 in tumor cells, enhancing MHC-I expression and tumour-intrinsic immunogenicity, thereby sensitizing tumors to T-cell-mediated killing. Inosine supplementation synergized with ICB in resistant mouse models (B16-GMCSF, 4T1). Clinical validation of the mechanism: Low UBA6 expression in human tumor tissues was associated with better progression-free survival in melanoma patients treated with anti-CTLA4 or anti-PD1, and lower UBA6 levels were found in responders (PR/SD) vs. non-responders (PD) in a small basket trial cohort (n=22). Limitations noted by authors: Direct measurement of inosine in the human clinical cohorts was not performed due to technical challenges (rapid degradation/clearance of adenosine/inosine in plasma), so the human data relies on retrospective metabolomic screening where inosine was one of many metabolites analyzed, and mechanistic validation is primarily preclinical.

The study provides extensive mechanistic context and contradictory evidence regarding metabolite levels. It details that SCFAs enhance immunotherapy efficacy via HDAC inhibition, GPR signaling, and mTOR pathway regulation, promoting CD8+ T cell cytotoxicity and cytokine production (IFN-γ, TNF-α) [65, 66, 67, 32]. However, it highlights a critical contradiction: high serum butyrate and propionate were negatively correlated with ICI efficacy in patients treated with anti-CTLA-4 (ipilimumab), and butyrate reduced CTLA-4 blockade efficacy in mouse models by inhibiting memory T cell accumulation and increasing Tregs [35]. Regarding Inosine, the study describes its mechanism in enhancing anti-CTLA-4 and anti-PD-L1 efficacy in mouse models via A2aR-cAMP-CREB signaling and Th1 differentiation, noting this effect is dependent on exogenous IFN-γ and CpG presence [72, 36]. For TMAO, the mechanism involves activating PERK-mediated ER stress and Gasdermin-E mediated pyroptosis to enhance CD8+ T cell immunity [37]. The review also lists other metabolites like Indoles (suppressing immunity via AhR in some contexts, promoting IL-22 in others) and Secondary Bile Acids (suppressing Th17 via ROR-γt inhibition) [39, 41, 44, 51].

The study reviews multiple clinical trials (Table 2) involving FMT and ICIs in melanoma, NSCLC, renal cell carcinoma, etc., but focuses on microbial composition (16S/metagenomics) rather than metabolite quantification.

The study highlights that many mechanistic insights (e.g., Inosine context-dependency, SCFA effects) are derived from mouse models or in vitro studies, with limited direct translation of concentration data to human clinical settings.
The study identifies gaps in standardizing responder definitions and extrapolating animal results to humans, which complicates the interpretation of any potential metabolite correlations.
